alternatives.option: A larger built-in catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: More coverage out of the box; each mode needs its own fidelity corpus and rubric, and custom modes already cover these.

alternatives.option: Ship an assistant mode that answers dictated questions
alternatives.tradeoff: An obvious use of a local language model; it is the behavior the requirements single out as a hazard, so it would have to declare `answersQuestions` and be visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

decisions.consequences: Built-ins are read-only; customizing one duplicates it into a user mode carrying the same contract as a starting point, which keeps the built-in fidelity corpus meaningful. Four modes means four rubric corpora per shipped language.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users routinely duplicate a built-in to make the same edit, which is evidence the built-in should change.

decisions.title: Automatic mode selection: ordered rules, specificity tiebreak, latched at arming
decisions.choice: An ordered rule list evaluated at arming, first match wins, ordered by the user, with specificity as the tiebreak within equal priority (URL host plus path prefix, then host, then bundle identifier, then any). The selected mode is latched into the run manifest. A predicate whose input cannot be obtained does not match, and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. The editor flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them.
decisions.rationale: First match on a user-ordered list is the model people know from mail filters and makes conflict resolution inspectable. Treating an unobtainable predicate as a non-match keeps a missing permission from producing a wrong mode. Latching at arming means the mode cannot change under the user mid-sentence.

alternatives.option: Highest specificity wins regardless of order
alternatives.tradeoff: No shadowed rules; the user cannot temporarily override a specific rule with a general one.

alternatives.option: Re-evaluate continuously during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Follows the user across windows; the mode could change mid-sentence and the run would no longer have one manifest.

alternatives.option: Infer the mode from what was said
alternatives.tradeoff: No rules to configure; requires recognition before mode selection, inverting the pipeline and making the current mode unpredictable.

decisions.consequences: The effective mode and whether it came from a rule or the fallback appear in the panel and menu bar for every run. Switching applications mid-recording keeps the mode chosen where the user started, consistent with the delivery latch. Browser URL availability varies and is enumerated per browser rather than assumed.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users regularly start recording, notice the wrong mode, and cancel, which would argue for a mode change during capture before recognition begins.

decisions.title: Vocabulary as staged passes with a defined order around recognition and generation
decisions.choice: Four stages in fixed order. (1) Recognition biasing: selected terms in the decoder prompt slot, capped to the runtime limit, chosen by mode relevance and recency. (2) Deterministic replacement over the recognition result: ordered rules, longest match first, boundary-aware using ICU word segmentation for the run's language, case-preserving, non-overlapping, applied once with no cascading. (3) Filler removal as a separate per-mode pass. (4) After generation, the replacement table is applied once more and the validator checks that vocabulary terms survived. Recognition and normalized results are both retained. For scripts without word spacing, replacement uses ICU segmentation where available and otherwise falls back to substring matching with a warning shown in the vocabulary editor.
decisions.rationale: The mechanisms fail differently and must not be conflated. Prompt biasing changes decoding probabilities and guarantees nothing, so the interface says so and never claims that adding a name makes it recognized. Deterministic replacement is exact and belongs on text. The post-generation pass exists because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word, and the user's spelling should win. Word boundaries are language-dependent, so the boundary rule names its mechanism rather than assuming spaces.

alternatives.option: Replacement only after generation
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; the generation stage then reasons over text containing mis-recognized terms.

alternatives.option: Replacement only before generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler; a model that alters a name in its output goes uncorrected.

alternatives.option: Ask the language model to apply the vocabulary
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles inflection and context that literal matching misses; makes an exact user-specified substitution probabilistic, which is the property users want here.

alternatives.option: Cascading replacement to a fixpoint
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles chained rules; introduces order-dependent results and possible loops for a rarely needed benefit.

decisions.consequences: Two texts per run to store and show. The editor must explain that terms have one probabilistic effect and one exact effect. The prompt slot forces selection when the vocabulary is large, so the panel can show which terms were included.
decisions.reconsider_when: A runtime exposes real biasing or constrained decoding, which moves exact-name handling into recognition.

decisions.title: Context sources: sampled at arming, budget-bounded, digest-only retention, framed as data
decisions.choice: Three optional sources sampled in parallel at arming against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection, and window title through accessibility (capped at 4000 characters); one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition (opt-in); the first text item on the pasteboard (capped). Anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to digest, length, and source kind; retaining text is opt-in per mode and deleted with the recording. In the prompt, context sits inside a per-run random delimiter, labeled reference material, with mode instructions before and the task restated after. Enforcement that context did not become instructions is the contract validator and its context n-gram check (D-012), with the fail-closed path as the bound on damage.
decisions.rationale: Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible; continuous sampling would make the same recording produce different prompts depending on timing. Digest-only retention keeps the library from accumulating copies of unrelated documents and screens while still letting a reprocess report that the original context is gone. Framing reduces instruction-following on context text without preventing it, which is why the validator rather than the framing carries the requirement.

alternatives.option: Sample at generation time
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresher context and screen recognition off the latency path; by then the user has often switched windows, so the sample describes somewhere they no longer are.

alternatives.option: Retain full context text by default
alternatives.tradeoff: Reprocessing reproduces the original result exactly; the library accumulates screen and clipboard contents by default, a privacy posture the product should not adopt quietly.

alternatives.option: Continuous screen sampling during capture
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures what changed while speaking; sustained recognition cost and a much larger retention question.

decisions.consequences: Screen recognition may routinely miss the deadline on busy displays and is then absent and noted. Reprocessing a recording whose context was not retained produces a different result, and History shows why. Injection resistance is defense in depth backed by the corpus in verification.
decisions.reconsider_when: Screen context proves valuable enough that users want it reliably, which moves sampling off the arming path and makes the rewrite stage wait for it.

decisions.title: Languages: per-mode selection or detection, translation as a derived result of a named recognition
decisions.choice: Each mode sets recognition language to an explicit code or auto. Auto uses the runtime's language identification with its probability; below threshold the run records `undetermined`, uses the mode's default language, and the panel says so. Translation to English is a separate declared operation producing a result whose `derived_from_result_id` names the exact recognition or normalized result it translated. Each model installation declares supported languages, labeled in the interface as declared by the publisher and unmeasured until an evaluation row exists.
decisions.rationale: Recognition quality and rewriting quality are different properties measured by different methods, so they are represented and evaluated separately. Naming the parent result is what makes translation provenance survive a second recognition of the same audio: without it, a translation of the first transcript looks equally like a translation of the second. Marking language support as declared keeps the product from promising coverage nobody measured.

alternatives.option: Always auto-detect
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to configure; short utterances and code-switching produce wrong detections and the user cannot pin a language they know.

alternatives.option: Translate by replacing the transcript
alternatives.tradeoff: One text per recording; the original wording is unrecoverable, breaking reprocessing and review.

alternatives.option: Translate as part of the rewrite
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass; translation and formatting become entangled and the validator cannot separate a translation error from a formatting one.

decisions.consequences: History shows several artifacts per recording and must make the parent of each obvious. A user-supplied model with an inaccurate manifest can overstate coverage, so the interface attributes the claim to the manifest. Rewriting in a language with no validator pack takes the fail-closed path from D-012, so multilingual recognition is broader than multilingual rewriting, and the interface says which.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured detection accuracy on short utterances makes auto safe as the default, or a runtime provides per-segment language identification supporting code-switching within a recording.

decisions.title: One ingest port carrying timing and flow control, with a declared format matrix
decisions.choice: All sources implement `AudioSource`, emitting `AudioFrame` values that carry stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence number, discontinuity flag, native sample rate, channel layout, and sample format. Conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono Float32 recognition input is an explicit stage after the port, not part of it. Consumers grant credit; a seekable source stops decoding when credit is exhausted, and a live source that overruns drops frames and records a discontinuity rather than buffering without bound. Microphone via AVAudioEngine, system audio via ScreenCaptureKit, files via AVAssetReader in 30-second windows. Initial matrix: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v, mov. Extension: a `DecoderProvider` port with an opt-in external command-line decoder adapter, off by default.
decisions.rationale: The earlier port emitted untimestamped canonical buffers, which cannot express what meetings need (two native streams aligned by host time, with drift and gaps visible) and cannot express backpressure, which is what actually bounds memory end to end. Windowed decoding bounds the decoder; credit bounds the queue between decoder, converter, and recognizer, including across the helper socket. RESEARCH notes whisper.cpp's example has input-format constraints, so an explicit decoding boundary is needed regardless.

alternatives.option: Canonical untimestamped buffers
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest consumer code; meeting alignment and gap reporting have to travel around the abstraction, and flow control has nowhere to live.

alternatives.option: Separate live and seekable ports
alternatives.tradeoff: Each expresses its own timing and retry rules; orchestration, cancellation, and conversion get duplicated between them.

alternatives.option: Decode whole files into memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest of all; a three-hour file at 16 kHz Float32 is roughly 700 MB before any model loads, which the requirements rule out.

alternatives.option: Bundle a general-purpose decoder
alternatives.tradeoff: Every format works out of the box; adds licensing obligations, binary size, and a security update duty for a decoder parsing untrusted files.

decisions.consequences: Every source carries timing metadata even when it has one stream and no drift. Live overrun is a visible discontinuity in the recording rather than a silent gap. The canonical conversion still discards content above 8 kHz for recognition, so imported originals are kept and meeting streams are sealed at native rate for any future use.
decisions.reconsider_when: A speech runtime benefits from a higher input rate, or the credit mechanism proves unnecessary because every runtime consumes faster than any source produces.

decisions.title: Imports are copy-in and commit-late, leaving the source untouched
decisions.choice: Import opens the source read-only, copies it into the session directory, and records a security-scoped bookmark for provenance. The recording row commits only when the artifact is complete and readable. On any failure the session directory is removed and no row exists. Moving the original happens only after commit, as a step the user can decline.
decisions.rationale: A failed import leaves its source unchanged if the import path never opens the source for writing and never deletes it. Committing after the artifact is complete keeps a failure from leaving a History entry pointing at nothing.

alternatives.option: Reference the source in place
alternatives.tradeoff: No duplication; the library breaks when the user moves or deletes the file, and reprocessing later finds nothing.

alternatives.option: Transcode on import and discard the original
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller library and one decode path; discards information and makes reprocessing with a better decoder impossible.

alternatives.option: Create the row first and fill it in
alternatives.tradeoff: Progress visible immediately; a failure leaves a broken row for recovery to reason about.

decisions.consequences: Imports duplicate storage, visible in the library size view and covered by retention. Large video imports copy the whole file though only the audio track is used; extracting only the audio is a refinement once the cost is measured.
decisions.reconsider_when: Large video imports become common enough that storing extracted audio plus a bookmark beats keeping the original.

decisions.title: Speech runtime selected at gate F1, with whisper.cpp as the reference adapter meanwhile
decisions.choice: Build against `SpeechRecognizer` with whisper.cpp as the reference adapter. Select the shipping runtime at gate F1 on measured word error rate, latency, helper RSS, checkpoint behavior, and a licensing review of the weights we would offer. Keep a second adapter only where F1 shows a role for it, specifically Intel coverage or a licensing outcome that blocks the primary.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH describes what each candidate documents and states plainly that documentation establishes neither accuracy nor resource behavior, while flagging licensing and long-recording suitability as unexamined. Committing to one runtime now would be a choice without evidence, and committing to maintain two permanently would pay for a hedge that may have no role once the measurement exists. Building against the port makes the choice a configuration outcome either way.

alternatives.option: whisper.cpp only, decided now
alternatives.tradeoff: One runtime, broad hardware coverage, no Swift package licensing question; C interop in the hot path and extra work for Core ML execution.

alternatives.option: WhisperKit only, decided now
alternatives.tradeoff: Best toolchain fit and least integration code; leaves Intel unsupported structurally and makes an unresolved licensing question load-bearing.

alternatives.option: Maintain both permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility; two parameter translations, two evaluation runs per model update, and two sets of capability descriptors to keep current.

alternatives.option: Apple's built-in speech recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: No models to manage; on-device availability and language coverage are controlled by the system and model choice is not exposed, which the requirements demand.

decisions.consequences: Results record which runtime produced them, so a change is visible in History. Until F1 completes, no accuracy or latency claim appears anywhere, and the scheduler uses its conservative preemption policy.
decisions.reconsider_when: F1 shows one runtime dominating on accuracy, latency, memory, and licensing, or an Intel requirement makes a second adapter necessary regardless.

decisions.title: Generation runtime: llama.cpp embedded in a helper, GGUF models
decisions.choice: Embed llama.cpp as a library in `dictation-llm-helper`, loading GGUF models with Metal on Apple Silicon and CPU otherwise, streaming tokens back over the socket pair. No server binary.
decisions.rationale: RESEARCH records llama.cpp as providing local inference with Metal support and both library integration material and server tooling, and asks that an embedded worker be compared with a local service including whether network access is possible. Embedding gives control over acquisition and lifecycle, and GGUF reaches the quantized models users already have, which matters because user-supplied models are in scope.

alternatives.option: MLX-based generation
alternatives.tradeoff: Apple-native with good Apple Silicon performance; a different model format, fewer ready quantizations, and no Intel path.

alternatives.option: Core ML converted models
alternatives.tradeoff: System-managed execution and no vendored C++; per-model conversion work, and user-supplied models become impractical.

alternatives.option: The llama.cpp server on localhost
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses upstream tooling; the reachability and forwarding concerns in D-003 apply directly.

decisions.consequences: Vendored C++ with build time, pinning, and update discipline. The helper is built for target architectures and signed with the bundle. Quantization becomes a user-visible setting with a memory consequence surfaced through D-027.
decisions.reconsider_when: MLX coverage of the quantizations users bring becomes comparable, or measured generation latency on the target is unacceptable and another runtime measurably beats it.

decisions.title: Model identity, immutable content-addressed installs, and transactional activation
decisions.choice: Identity is (publisher name, revision string, SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set). Installation stages into `Models/.staging/<uuid>`, verifies per-file and set hashes, runs a load smoke test in a helper against the staged path, then renames the directory to `Models/blobs/<setHash>`, a path that never previously existed and is never written again; if that path already exists, the content is already installed and staging is deleted. A single SQLite transaction then inserts the installation row and updates the active pointer. Runs hold a lease on the installation they pinned, so activation changes never remove weights under a running job. Garbage collection removes blobs with no installation row and no live lease, at launch and after lease release. Compatibility is checked before activation against the runtime descriptor: runtime kind, version range, quantization support, sample rate, context length. Runtimes receive absolute paths and never load by name.
decisions.rationale: The earlier sequence spanned a filesystem rename and a database update with no ordering rule and renamed over a live directory, so a crash could leave an installed directory with no row or a pointer to files being replaced. Immutable content-addressed blobs make installation idempotent and make the only mutable state a database pointer that moves inside one transaction. Hashing weights rather than trusting a name is what makes "the same model" checkable across a rename or a re-download, and the smoke test catches the common user-supplied failure at install rather than mid-dictation. RESEARCH warns that a default runtime initialization may download models, so passing explicit paths is the enforcement point.

alternatives.option: Identity by file name or publisher identifier
alternatives.tradeoff: No hashing cost on multi-gigabyte files; two quantizations under one name become indistinguishable in History.

alternatives.option: Install in place and roll back on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: No staging space needed; a failure during the write leaves a corrupt live model, the outcome the requirement forbids.

alternatives.option: Versioned slots with an activation journal
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps old and new side by side without content addressing; recovery logic is more involved and duplicate content is stored twice.

alternatives.option: Let the runtime's own downloader manage models
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less code; hands acquisition to a component that may download implicitly, breaking the offline contract.

decisions.consequences: Installation needs free space for the staged and the stored copy, checked before starting. Hashing large files takes time and is shown as a verification step. Blobs can outlive their rows briefly after a crash and are collected at launch. Failed user imports stay in staging with the error attached until dismissed.
decisions.reconsider_when: Hashing time becomes a usability problem, which argues for incremental hashing during download, or leases show contention patterns that make a different pinning scheme preferable.

decisions.title: Meetings: channel origin as fact, speaker attribution as hypothesis, notes with citations
decisions.choice: Record microphone and system audio as separate artifacts with `role` recorded as a capture fact and aligned by host time. The interface labels them microphone channel and system audio channel rather than naming people. Diarization produces per-segment hypotheses (cluster, embedding, confidence, and evidence including channel energy ratio and cross-channel correlation); segments below the confidence threshold are unattributed. Segments whose microphone content correlates with delayed system audio are marked as probable echo and excluded from microphone-side attribution. Speaker names attach to `speaker_identities` holding centroid embeddings captured at naming time; after re-running diarization, new clusters match identities by embedding similarity, and matches below the threshold are presented for confirmation rather than applied. Notes are generated by a built-in mode over the timestamped transcript in overlapping windows, each bullet citing a segment range, with uncited bullets dropped in the reduce pass. Diarization is unavailable until a diarizer is selected, licensed, and evaluated; meetings ship with channel labels until then.
decisions.rationale: A microphone can pick up remote audio from speakers and system audio can carry several applications, so channel origin is a fact about capture and says less about who spoke than the earlier design implied. Cluster numbers are arbitrary across runs, so carrying user-edited names on numeric identity would silently misattribute after re-clustering; embeddings plus confirmation is the honest mapping. Confidence and an unattributed label are in the schema because the requirement forbids treating identity as certain when evidence is insufficient. RESEARCH names SpeakerKit within the Argmax package and notes its default initialization may download models, so its acquisition goes through the model store.

alternatives.option: Diarize a single mixed recording
alternatives.tradeoff: One file and one capture path; discards the channel signal entirely and makes even the easiest question an inference.

alternatives.option: Treat channels as speaker identity
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple labels users understand immediately; wrong whenever speakers leak into the microphone or several people share a room.

alternatives.option: Assign every segment to the nearest cluster
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean-looking transcripts; confidently wrong attributions in notes, the failure the requirements call out.

alternatives.option: Generate notes in one pass over the whole transcript
alternatives.tradeoff: Better global structure; exceeds context on long meetings and gives no way to check a bullet against the audio.

decisions.consequences: Two artifacts per meeting and roughly double the storage, at native rate. Echo detection is a design provision whose thresholds come from evaluation, not from this document. Dropping uncited bullets can remove a correct line that failed to cite, so the drop rate is tracked. Diarization ships later than meeting capture, which is visible in the phase plan.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured diarization on mixed audio approaches channel-separated results, or no candidate diarizer exposes usable confidence, in which case meetings stay channel-only.

decisions.title: History: append-only results over identified runs, full-text search, tombstones with generation tokens
decisions.choice: History lists recordings, each expandable into its processing runs and their result chains. Search is FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets. Playback uses the sealed artifact. Reprocessing creates a run and inserts results; nothing is mutated, and a user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter, and signals cancellation; every worker carries (recording id, generation) from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned, or at a different generation. Hard deletion happens when the last lease releases or at the next launch sweep.
decisions.rationale: A late worker response cannot recreate a deleted recording only if the existence check and the insert are the same transaction; any check-then-insert has a window. The generation counter covers delete-then-recreate at the same identifier. Organizing the list by run is what makes reprocessing through a different speech model comparable rather than confusing, since each run names the models and mode revision that produced its chain.

alternatives.option: Hard delete immediately and let workers fail
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone bookkeeping; a constraint violation becomes the race outcome and scratch files are orphaned.

alternatives.option: Cancel workers and wait for acknowledgement before deleting
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone state; the user's delete blocks on a worker mid-window, and a hung worker blocks it indefinitely.

alternatives.option: Overwrite results on reprocessing
alternatives.tradeoff: One result per recording and a simpler list; comparing a new model against the old becomes impossible, which is a stated use of reprocessing.

decisions.consequences: Deleted recordings hold disk until leases release, so the interface says deleting rather than claiming reclaimed space. FTS triggers must handle result deletion, covered by tests. A recording with several runs needs a detail view that makes each run's recognition and current result obvious at a glance.
decisions.reconsider_when: Result rows dominate database size, which argues for storing older results compressed or on disk rather than inline.

decisions.title: Desktop behavior: menu bar surface, software input gain, media pause with manual resume
decisions.choice: An NSStatusItem shows state, current mode, recent results, and settings. Microphone level is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in. Media pausing checks whether the default output device is running before capture and posts a play-pause key when it is. Resume is a user action offered in the panel and menu for ten minutes after recording. Automatic resume is opt-in and fires only if the app posted the pause, the same output device is still default, the device is still idle, and under ten minutes have elapsed. Device volume is restored only if the current value still equals the value the app set.
decisions.rationale: The app can observe that some client is running on the output device and can post a media key; neither identifies the application that reacted or confirms that anything paused. Automatic resume built on that evidence can start playback the user stopped by hand. Offering resume as an action keeps the convenience while removing the wrong-action failure, and users who accept the risk can enable automatic resume with its conditions stated. Software gain changes no system setting, so the default has no restore obligation at all.

alternatives.option: Automatic resume on by default under the ownership conditions
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to click after recording; the conditions cannot establish which application received the key, so it can resume something the user stopped deliberately.

alternatives.option: Private MediaRemote framework for playback state and control
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate per-application state and precise control; an undocumented interface that can break on any OS update and complicates notarization posture.

alternatives.option: Per-application scripting for known players
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise for Music, Spotify, and similar; needs automation permission per application and covers only an enumerated list.

alternatives.option: Do not touch media playback
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to get wrong; leaves background audio bleeding into recordings, which the requirement asks to address.

decisions.consequences: Users get a Resume control rather than automatic restoration unless they opt in, and the menu states that the app cannot confirm which application it addressed. Software gain cannot rescue a signal clipped at the hardware, which the clipping indicator surfaces so the user can lower device gain.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API supplies target identity and confirms the pause transition, at which point automatic resume can become the default for confirmed targets.

decisions.title: Shortcuts: distinct toggle and push-to-talk bindings, evidence-based stuck-key recovery, no duration cap
decisions.choice: A single `ShortcutRegistrar` owns a session-level consuming `CGEventTap` handling keyDown, keyUp, and flagsChanged. Toggle and push-to-talk are separate bindings; a combination may be bound to at most one of them, validated at bind time. Toggle acts on keyDown and ignores keyUp. Push-to-talk starts on keyDown and finalizes on keyUp, with an optional per-binding tap-to-lock: a keyUp within a configurable window (default 250 ms) latches recording until the next press. Lost key-up is recovered from evidence rather than elapsed time: tap-disabled notifications, screen lock and sleep notifications, and a 1 Hz poll of the physical key state that finalizes when the key reports up while the app believes it is down. There is no maximum recording duration. Per-mode bindings are toggle or push-to-talk bindings with a mode attached. `kCGEventTapDisabledByTimeout` re-enables the tap. Without the tap, toggle falls back to Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey` and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation.
decisions.rationale: The earlier design overloaded one binding with a 200 ms hold discriminator, which left the first 200 ms undefined and made a short press ambiguous, and it capped a held recording at a configured maximum, which is a recording-duration limit the specification prohibits. Separate bindings remove the ambiguity, and polling the physical key state addresses the real problem (a key-up the tap never delivered) with evidence about that key rather than with a timer that also truncates valid speech.

alternatives.option: One binding with a hold discriminator
alternatives.tradeoff: One combination to configure; the first hold window has undefined behavior and a slow keyboard repeat or a dropped event changes the meaning of a press.

alternatives.option: Carbon RegisterEventHotKey only
alternatives.tradeoff: No Accessibility permission and reliable consumption; no key-up, so push-to-talk cannot exist.

alternatives.option: NSEvent global monitors only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple API with no tap lifecycle; events cannot be consumed, so the hotkey also reaches the foreground application.

alternatives.option: A maximum hold watchdog
alternatives.tradeoff: Guarantees a stuck key eventually stops recording; truncates a genuinely long push-to-talk recording, which the specification forbids.

decisions.consequences: The app sits on the keyboard event path, so its handler must stay fast or the tap is disabled by timeout, which the re-enable path treats as a monitored condition. Users configure two shortcuts instead of one. The key-state poll runs only while a push-to-talk recording is active.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API provides global hotkeys with key-up, or the poll proves unreliable for remapped or external keyboards, which would argue for a visible stuck-key banner with a stop control instead.

decisions.title: Model residency under a declared budget that measurement replaces
decisions.choice: Budget the application at 8 GB peak on the 16 GB target, counting app and helper processes. At most one speech and one generation model resident, unloaded after ten idle minutes. Activation of a pairing whose footprint exceeds the budget is refused with the arithmetic shown, the refusal stating whether its numbers are measured or declared, and an explicit override available. Once F1 descriptors exist, admission uses measured peak RSS and Metal heap peak per installation rather than declared file sizes.
decisions.rationale: The specification forbids artificial quotas and requires honest reporting of limits, which is different from ignoring the ceiling: swap on a 16 GB machine turns a latency problem into a system-wide stall. Declared weight sizes omit runtime workspaces, Metal allocations, and helper overhead, so a refusal computed from them can deny a pairing that would have worked. Labeling the basis and keeping the override means the policy never becomes a limit the user cannot see through.

alternatives.option: Load on demand with no residency limit
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fastest where memory allows; on the stated target a large pairing plus a browser drives the machine into swap.

alternatives.option: Keep selected models resident permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest per-run latency; several gigabytes held while the app idles in the menu bar.

alternatives.option: Rely on memory pressure notifications alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to real conditions; reacts after the stall has started.

decisions.consequences: First use after idle pays a model load shown as a loading state. Until descriptors exist the budget is arithmetic that can be wrong in either direction, which the refusal text says. Memory pressure notifications still trigger early unload of idle models.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured residency differs materially from declared sizes, or the app runs on machines where the ceiling does not bind.

decisions.title: Egress control scoped to what the design can enforce
decisions.choice: Inference helpers contain no networking code; build checks assert that helper targets and their SPM dependency closure import no networking modules and that linked binaries reference no socket or CFNetwork symbols; a network-denied integration test runs a full session. Model downloads happen only on explicit user action through a separate downloader restricted to an allowlist of model hosts and writing only into staging. Runtime initializers that can download are prohibited by a static check, and runtimes always receive absolute local paths. The external decoder is off by default; enabling it states that the app cannot constrain a binary the user selects, names the binary in settings, and disables it when the strict offline configuration is on. The product claim is that the inference path contains and exercises no network code, verified by build checks and a network-denied session, and it strengthens to system-enforced denial only if gate F2 finds a workable process restriction.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires that audio, transcripts, and context stay on the Mac and that model loading not trigger downloads, and RESEARCH notes that a diarization runtime's default initialization may download models. Structural absence of network code plus a denied-network test is verifiable. A symbol scan cannot prove that a linked framework or dynamically loaded code makes no request, and it says nothing about a user-selected executable, so the claim is stated at the strength the evidence supports rather than as an absolute.

alternatives.option: Claim system-enforced isolation now
alternatives.tradeoff: A stronger statement users would like; the mechanism is unproven on the baseline and the specification's own open question records that.

alternatives.option: Allow runtimes to fetch missing models
alternatives.tradeoff: Better first run with no model manager; makes network access a side effect of loading a model, which the requirements forbid.

alternatives.option: Ship no downloader and require manual placement
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee and least code; makes first run considerably harder and pushes users toward downloading models through less careful means.

alternatives.option: Remove the external decoder entirely
alternatives.tradeoff: No trust transfer to an unconstrained binary; users with opus in matroska have no path at all until a decoder is bundled.

decisions.consequences: The downloader is a separate component with its own tests. Users wanting a model outside the allowlist import it locally through the same verification. Enabling the external decoder is a documented trust transfer rather than a sandboxed operation, and the strict offline configuration turns it off.
decisions.reconsider_when: F2 finds an enforceable restriction, in which case both the helper claim and the decoder story change, or a bundled decoder becomes justified by demand.

decisions.title: Processing runs as the provenance spine of every derived artifact
decisions.choice: Introduce `processing_runs` between recordings and results. Every result belongs to a run and names its immediate input through `derived_from_result_id`; recognition results are chain roots and carry the speech model installation that produced them. A recording may hold several recognition results, one per recognition run. Results are immutable after insert, enforced by a trigger.
decisions.rationale: The earlier design gave a recording exactly one source transcript while also allowing reprocessing through a different speech model. Those cannot both hold: after a second recognition, a translation or rewrite has no way to say which words it came from, and the invariant that the source transcript is never mutated hides a replacement behind a supposedly unique row. Making the run the unit that pins settings and owns a chain answers provenance with a foreign key rather than with inference.

alternatives.option: Keep one transcript per recording and forbid re-recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: The simplest graph and the shortest History view; removes reprocessing through another speech model, which the requirements ask for.

alternatives.option: Version the transcript in place with a revision counter
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer rows than runs; older derived results end up pointing at a version that no longer matches the displayed text.

alternatives.option: Attach model ids to results and infer parentage by timestamp
alternatives.tradeoff: No new table; parentage becomes a guess that breaks whenever two runs overlap, which the batch lane makes routine.

decisions.consequences: More joins in History queries and a detail view that presents runs rather than a flat result list. Reprocessing gains a clear entry stage, since a text reprocess names its parent result and skips recognition. The FTS index carries results from every run, so search can return two recognitions of the same audio, which the result rows disambiguate.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users never re-recognize, which would make the run table pure overhead, though the same structure is what makes translations and notes attributable.

decisions.title: Crash-safe capture through an fsynced chunk journal with incremental sealing
decisions.choice: Capture writes fixed-period chunks (default two seconds) of headerless native-rate PCM, each written to a `.part` file, fsynced, renamed, with the directory fsynced. A sealer encodes completed chunks into the ALAC artifact, appends `(chunk, packets, offset)` to an fsynced index, and deletes chunks it has durably encoded. At capture end the packet table is written from the index and the artifact is fsynced and hashed. Recovery rebuilds the packet table from the index, truncates to the last durable extent, and appends surviving chunks.
decisions.rationale: The earlier design asserted that a partially written ALAC-in-CAF file could be finalized after SIGKILL, with no experiment and no journal format behind it, and the verification suite then asserted recovery outcomes that depended on that assertion. Recovery here depends only on records the app writes and fsyncs itself. The worst-case loss is the unsealed tail, bounded by the chunk period plus unflushed data within it, and the exact figure comes from the kill-at-offset experiment rather than from this document.

alternatives.option: Write the container directly and rely on it being recoverable
alternatives.tradeoff: No journal, no sealer, no extra fsyncs; the recovery story rests on an untested property of a container that stores its packet table at the end.

alternatives.option: Keep raw PCM as the only durable form until the run completes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest recovery; transient storage equals the full raw recording, which for a three-hour two-stream meeting is several gigabytes.

alternatives.option: Write a second copy of the container periodically
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovery reads the last complete copy; doubles write volume and still loses everything since the last copy.

decisions.consequences: An fsync every chunk period and a sealer to maintain, plus roughly a 30-second window of journal files alongside the artifact during long captures. Chunk period is the tuning knob between recovery loss and write frequency. Sealing is idempotent, which is what makes recovery from the `sealing` state safe.
decisions.reconsider_when: The kill-at-offset experiment shows a loss bound the product cannot live with, or a container format with an incrementally durable index removes the need for a separate journal.

decisions.title: A state-indexed recovery contract with an explicit durability ordering rule
decisions.choice: Every non-terminal run state has an authoritative recovery transition (listed in the data lifecycle), and the ordering rule is written down: a durable record of intent precedes an externally visible irreversible effect, while a locally idempotent effect is followed by its commit. Recovery may complete deterministic stages such as refining, and never resumes generation or delivery without user action.
decisions.rationale: The earlier sweep defined arming, capturing, delivery attempts, scratch, and staging, while verification asserted recovery outcomes at every stage boundary. That gap would be filled by whichever test author reached it first, which is exactly the deferral the specification prohibits. Naming the ordering rule also makes new stages easy to place correctly instead of case by case.

alternatives.option: Discard any run that was in flight at a crash
alternatives.tradeoff: One rule and no partial state; throws away a completed recognition because the app crashed during a rewrite.

alternatives.option: Resume every in-flight run automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Least user friction; re-runs generation the user may no longer want and risks re-delivering into whatever is now focused.

alternatives.option: Ask the user at launch what to do with each interrupted run
alternatives.tradeoff: No wrong default; a dialog listing interrupted work at every launch after a crash is a poor first impression and invites blind dismissal.

decisions.consequences: Recovery does deterministic work automatically and stops at anything that consumes a model or touches another application. Behavior tables must cover every state, and the crash-injection suite asserts against them rather than against improvised expectations.
decisions.reconsider_when: A new stage appears whose effects are neither externally visible nor idempotent, which would need a rule of its own rather than a case in this table.

decisions.title: Permissions as a capability-by-state matrix
decisions.choice: Replace the single revocation outcome with a matrix over (capability, run state, active adapter). Losing microphone or an active system-audio stream terminates capture; losing Accessibility affects insertion and shortcut consumption but not recognition; losing Input Monitoring affects shortcuts; losing browser automation affects URL predicates; losing Screen Recording ends screen context and system-audio capture while leaving microphone capture running. Denial at launch, revocation during work, and restoration each have a defined effect, and restoration is reported once.
decisions.rationale: The earlier text mapped every revocation to `failed(capturing, permissionRevoked)`, which would end a valid recording because the user changed a delivery permission during recognition, and would report a lost shortcut permission as an audio failure. Capabilities serve different stages, so their loss belongs at those stages.

alternatives.option: One global failure state
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to implement and explain; stops work that is still valid and misreports the cause.

alternatives.option: Ignore revocation until the capability is next used
alternatives.tradeoff: No mid-run interruption; the user gets a confusing failure later with no connection to the change they made.

decisions.consequences: The matrix is longer than a rule and is directly testable, and it becomes part of the approved behavior tables. Each capability needs a probe and a change notification path.
decisions.reconsider_when: A capability appears whose loss affects several stages differently enough that the matrix needs a third dimension beyond adapter identity.

decisions.title: One artifact lease protocol shared by workers, playback, export, and retention
decisions.choice: A `leases` table records holder, artifact, acquisition, and heartbeat. Acquiring a lease requires the recording row to exist, be untombstoned, and match the expected generation. Workers, the audio player, exports, and every retention policy acquire leases. Retention skips recordings with a live lease and retries on the next pass. Discarding audio is a distinct `audio_discarded` state that disables playback and re-recognition while leaving text reprocessing available. Stale leases are reclaimed at launch and by a sweeper.
decisions.rationale: The earlier design gave user-initiated deletion a tombstone and generation protocol and then introduced age, size, and audio-only retention jobs that did not participate in it, so a daily policy could remove the artifact under an admitted job or during playback and leave History offering playback that no longer works. One protocol for every consumer removes the class rather than the instance.

alternatives.option: Retention as immediate deletion with best-effort cancellation
alternatives.tradeoff: Policies always run on schedule; a race with an admitted job produces a failure whose outcome depends on timing.

alternatives.option: Quiesce all work before retention runs
alternatives.tradeoff: No leases needed; a long import blocks retention indefinitely, and retention blocks new work while it runs.

alternatives.option: Reference counting in memory only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper than a table; counts vanish on a crash, so recovery cannot tell which artifacts were in use.

decisions.consequences: Every consumer of an artifact must acquire and heartbeat a lease, including playback, which is more ceremony than a player usually needs. Retention can lag when a recording stays busy, which is reported rather than forced. Lease reclamation is part of the launch sweep.
decisions.reconsider_when: Lease contention delays retention long enough to matter, which would argue for pausing playback and preempting batch work rather than deferring.

decisions.title: A feasibility phase precedes freezing ports, schema, and the offline claim
decisions.choice: Phase F runs four spikes before phase 0: the speech runtime harness, helper isolation, the kill-at-offset capture experiment, and the insertion prototype. Each phase after it declares entry gates, persisted-schema work, the failure cases it covers, exit evidence, the approver of that evidence, and what rolling it back costs.
decisions.rationale: Four decisions in this design depend on properties nothing has measured: which runtime ships and whether it can checkpoint, whether an operating-system restriction can enforce the offline claim, how much audio a crash costs, and which applications allow confirmable insertion. Scheduling them after the ports and schema that depend on them would mean a negative result invalidates work already built on it. The specification also names a complete phased implementation plan as part of the deliverable, and a feature ordering without gates or evidence is not that.

alternatives.option: Start the skeleton immediately and measure in later phases
alternatives.tradeoff: Visible progress sooner; a negative F1 or F3 result forces rework of the ingest port, the scheduler, and the capture writer.

alternatives.option: Prototype everything end to end before designing
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum evidence before commitment; delays every requirement that does not depend on the unknowns.

alternatives.option: Treat the unknowns as risks accepted at implementation time
alternatives.tradeoff: No spike phase to schedule; hands behavioral decisions to whichever task hits them, which the specification forbids.

decisions.consequences: Roughly one phase of work produces no shippable feature, only descriptors, matrices, bounds, and decision updates. Each later phase has an entry gate that can block it, which makes dependencies visible and occasionally idle. Phase F outputs are inputs to D-001, D-004, D-009, D-020, D-027, D-028, and D-030.
decisions.reconsider_when: A spike's fallback proves acceptable enough that the spike itself is not worth its cost, which is a judgment to record rather than to assume.

decisions.title: Named approval authority and specification traceability for expected behavior
decisions.choice: Expected behavior lives in `docs/behavior/` tables whose rows each cite a SPEC.md clause or are marked derived. The normative approver is the user as product owner, or a delegate named in `docs/behavior/OWNERS`. Approval of a table gates writing tests against it; tests reference row identifiers; changing an approved row requires re-approval recorded in git history. Independent authorship of tables remains a hygiene rule and is not the authority.
decisions.rationale: A passing test proves only that the code met its assertions, so the assertions need an owner who can say they are the intended product behavior. The earlier design required review by someone other than the author, which does not establish product authority or fidelity to the specification. Clause citations make it possible to check that a requirement was followed into the design rather than paraphrased.

alternatives.option: Peer review by any team member
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and fast; two people can share the same misreading of a requirement with nobody empowered to settle it.

alternatives.option: Treat SPEC.md as the only source and skip behavior tables
alternatives.tradeoff: No second artifact to maintain; the specification does not enumerate state and event pairs, so implementers fill the gaps silently.

alternatives.option: Derive expectations from the implementation and review the diff
alternatives.tradeoff: Least documentation work; makes the code its own specification, which is the failure this decision exists to prevent.

decisions.consequences: Phases cannot exit until their tables are approved, which puts the product owner on the critical path. Derived rows are visible as a category, so the volume of behavior with no specification basis stays measurable.
decisions.reconsider_when: Approval becomes the dominant delay, which would argue for pre-approved templates for mechanical tables rather than for removing the gate.

coverage.explanation: Global toggle and push-to-talk from another application come from one session-level event tap that observes key-up and consumes the hotkey (D-026). Toggle and push-to-talk are separate configurable bindings, so a press has one meaning and no hold window is ambiguous; per-mode bindings select a mode and start a run in one action, with in-app conflict detection at bind time and a test-press step for system conflicts. A lost key-up is recovered from tap-disabled and screen-lock notifications and from polling the physical key state, so there is no maximum hold and no recording-duration cap of any kind. Without Accessibility or Input Monitoring the tap cannot run, so toggle falls back to a Carbon hotkey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation rather than failing silently (D-032). Cancellation has a defined effect at every stage (D-007) because stages are explicit run states (D-006): arming discards, capturing discards the journal by default, recognizing keeps audio and saves no partial transcript, refining drops the normalized result, rewriting keeps it and offers it, and delivering is cancellable only before the first event is posted. A crash mid-run resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract rather than through improvised handling (D-031).

The processed transcript is inserted at the caret or over the current selection by setting `AXSelectedText`; the app never sets an element's whole value, so a field's existing contents are preserved (D-009). Where that path is unavailable, the pasteboard path posts Command-V and reads the target's state back when it is readable, treating an observed change as delivered and an observed absence as rejected; synthesized typing is attempted only after an observed rejection, and a target with no readable state gets one unconfirmed attempt and no retry. Optional submission uses the modifier sampled at stop and posts Return only when delivery reached the latched element through a path that posted events. The target is latched at arming with its insertion capability, and focus changes have explicit outcomes: same element delivers, same application with a different element delivers by default, another application holds with Deliver and Copy, a departed application holds (D-008). Clipboard changes are handled by snapshotting before writing and restoring after the outcome is known, only while the change count is ours, deferred by a per-application profile for unconfirmed outcomes, and skipped entirely for targets that read the pasteboard late or for content that cannot be snapshotted, with the user told before anything is written. Permissions denied or revoked route the result to History and the pasteboard through the capability matrix rather than ending the run (D-032), and secure input suppresses synthesis entirely. Duplicate delivery is prevented structurally: the attempt row commits before any event is posted, and pending, posted, and unconfirmed attempts become needs_review at launch and are never re-posted (D-010).

A provisional live transcript comes from a separate low-priority pass over a sliding window and a waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed allocation-free on the capture thread (D-011). The compact window is a non-activating, borderless panel at status-bar level that joins all spaces, is movable by its background, and never becomes key, so showing it cannot break the delivery latch. Placement is remembered as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier and is clamped to the primary display when either is gone. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label and is replaced by the final transcript with a change highlight; the provisional stream is never persisted as a result, because it was produced over partial context and is a different artifact from the recognition result the run commits (D-006). Recording and processing failures appear as a panel row with a short reason and one action, including the case where the scheduler declines the provisional pass while batch work holds the speech model, which shows as preview paused rather than as a stalled transcript (D-004). Whether the provisional pass can run without costing dropped buffers or final quality is measured in phase 2, and the degraded presentation already has a defined state.

Four built-in modes cover ordinary dictation and task-specific output: Standard, Email, Note, and Meeting notes (D-013). Each carries a structured transformation contract rather than a prose description: Standard is limited to punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal, and vocabulary substitution; Email adds template salutation and sign-off, paragraph structure, and register adjustment with no new factual content; Note adds list and heading structure; Meeting notes permits summarization because that is its purpose and is bounded by a citation requirement instead of a recall threshold. All four declare that they do not answer questions, and the validator enforces that interrogatives in the normalized transcript survive in order, that expansion stays within the mode's limit, that content-word recall clears the threshold, and that no long span appears which is present in the context block and absent from the transcript (D-012). A failure retries once with a stricter instruction and then falls back to the normalized transcript, marked as a validator fallback. In a language with no validator pack for the mode, the generation stage is skipped and the normalized transcript is used, so the prohibition on answering never depends on an unenforced check. A mode that answered dictated questions would have to declare that in its contract, which also makes it visibly distinct in the mode indicator.

Users author prompts and formatting rules, and each custom mode also fills in a structured transformation contract naming its allowed operations, whether it may answer questions, its content bound, and the languages its validator supports; the editor cannot save a mode without one, because a free-form prompt gives the validator nothing to check against (D-012). Each mode selects its own local speech and language models by content identity rather than by name (D-022). Every save creates a content-addressed revision in an append-only chain, and every run pins the revision id into its manifest at start along with model installations, vocabulary revision, language, and validator pack (D-006). Work already in progress reads its snapshot rather than live settings, so editing a mode or switching models during a recognition cannot change what the running job produces. Saved results keep pointing at the revision that produced them, and History names that revision and diffs it against the current one, so a later edit cannot silently change the meaning of an earlier result. Because every result also names the run and the parent result it derives from (D-029), a rewrite produced by an old revision remains attributable even after the audio is recognized again under a different model.

Rules match the foreground application's bundle identifier and, where readable, the website URL, evaluated once at arming with first match winning over a user-ordered list (D-014). Conflicts resolve by that order, with specificity as the tiebreak within equal priority, and the editor flags rules that can never fire because an earlier rule shadows them. When a predicate's input cannot be obtained, because browser automation is denied, the browser exposes no URL, or screen recording is off, rules needing that input do not match and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. Permission loss is handled per capability, so losing browser automation narrows rule matching without disturbing capture or recognition (D-032). The chosen mode is latched into the run manifest, so it cannot change mid-sentence, and the effective mode plus whether it came from a rule or the fallback appears in the recording panel and the menu bar for every run, which is what keeps the current mode apparent (D-011). Which browsers expose a URL is enumerated in a dated matrix during phase 6 rather than assumed, and an incomplete matrix degrades to bundle-identifier rules.

User terminology and names enter at four points with a fixed order relative to recognition and language processing (D-015). Before recognition, selected terms go into the decoder's prompt slot, bounded by the runtime's limit and chosen by mode relevance and recency; this shifts decoding probabilities and the interface says exactly that, with no claim that adding a name guarantees recognition, because the mechanism is a prompt rather than a decoding constraint (D-020). After recognition, configurable replacements run deterministically over the recognition result with longest-match-first, boundary-aware, case-preserving, non-overlapping, single-pass semantics, using ICU word segmentation for the run's language and falling back to substring matching with a warning for scripts where segmentation is unavailable. Filler removal is a separate per-mode pass after replacement. After generation the replacement table is applied once more and the validator checks that vocabulary terms survived (D-012), because a language model will sometimes normalize an unusual proper noun back to a common word and the user's spelling should win. Recognition and normalized results are both retained, so the effect of each stage is inspectable, and where no validator pack exists the run takes the fail-closed path and delivers the normalized text with its replacements applied.

Three optional sources are sampled at arming in parallel against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection, and window title through accessibility; one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition when opted in; and the first text item on the pasteboard, each capped (D-016). Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible; anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Retention defaults to a digest, byte length, and source kind rather than the text, so the library does not accumulate copies of unrelated documents and screens, while a later reprocess can still report that the original context is unavailable; retaining text is opt-in per mode, shown in History, and deleted with the recording. Missing permissions leave a named operating state rather than a broken app: no Screen Recording means no screen context and no system audio while everything else continues, and losing Accessibility removes focused-element context without ending an in-flight run (D-032). Context is supplied as data, fenced in a per-run random delimiter and labeled reference material with mode instructions before it and the task restated after. Framing alone does not constrain a model, so the requirement that context must not override processing instructions is carried by the contract validator, including the check that rejects any span of eight or more tokens present in the context and absent from the transcript, with the fail-closed fallback to the normalized transcript when validation is unavailable (D-012). Context never leaves the machine: it crosses only the local socket pair to a helper that contains no network code, verified by build checks and a network-denied session test (D-028).

Recognition language is set per mode to an explicit code or to detection using the runtime's language identification with its probability; below the threshold the run records undetermined, uses the mode's default, and the panel says so (D-017). Translation into English is a separate declared operation that inserts a result naming the exact recognition or normalized result it translated, so the source transcript is preserved beside any derived text and stays identifiable even after the same audio is recognized again under a different model (D-029). Recognition and rewriting are evaluated by different methods and reported separately, word error rate for the first and a human rubric for the second, because a rewrite score cannot distinguish a mis-recognized word from a badly reworded sentence. Compatibility is declared per model installation and checked against the runtime descriptor at activation (D-022); the interface attributes language claims to the model publisher and marks them unmeasured until an evaluation row exists, so no coverage is promised on documentation alone. Rewriting is additionally limited by validator pack coverage: a mode and language pair with no pack takes the fail-closed path and delivers the normalized transcript unless the user sets a per-mode override that is recorded on the result (D-012), so multilingual recognition is broader than multilingual rewriting and the interface states which.

Microphone, system audio, and imported audio and video all implement one `AudioSource` that emits native-format frames carrying stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence, and a discontinuity flag, with conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono recognition input as an explicit stage after the port (D-018). Consumers grant credit, so a seekable source stops decoding when the recognizer falls behind and a live source that overruns records a discontinuity instead of buffering without bound; that is what bounds memory across the app and the helper rather than the decoder alone. The initial format matrix is what the system decoders cover: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v, and mov. The extension mechanism is a `DecoderProvider` port with an opt-in external command-line decoder that is off by default and carries an explicit statement that the app cannot constrain a binary the user selects (D-028). Files decode in 30-second windows, and the memory claim is tested as a slope across 10-minute, 1-hour, and 3-hour imports measured in both the app and the recognition helper, since a single run in one process cannot establish independence from duration. A failed import leaves its source unchanged because the path opens it read-only, copies into the session directory, and commits only after the artifact is complete; on failure the directory is removed and no row exists (D-019). Imports run in the batch lane and yield to interactive dictation under the scheduler's preemption policy for the runtime in use (D-004).

A meeting captures microphone and system audio as two artifacts whose frames carry host-time stamps, so alignment and gaps are represented by the ingest port rather than reconstructed afterwards (D-018). Channel origin is recorded as a fact about capture and labeled as the microphone channel and the system audio channel; it is not presented as speaker identity, because a microphone can pick up remote audio from speakers and a system stream can carry several applications (D-023). Diarization attaches per-segment hypotheses with confidence and evidence, segments below the threshold are unattributed rather than assigned, and segments whose microphone content correlates with delayed system audio are marked as probable echo and excluded from microphone-side attribution. Editing speaker names writes to identities holding centroid embeddings, so a rename never alters model output and a later diarization run matches identities by embedding similarity with confirmation for weak matches, rather than by cluster numbers that are arbitrary across runs. Timestamped notes are generated locally over the diarized transcript in overlapping windows sized to the language model's context, each bullet citing a segment range and uncited bullets dropped. Runtime choices are explicit: which diarizer is installed and which language model generates notes, both under the residency budget so a long meeting does not drive the machine into swap (D-027). Capture is crash-safe through the chunk journal, so an interrupted meeting yields a sealed artifact per stream with a bounded tail loss rather than an unreadable file (D-030). Evaluation methods are named and unperformed, so no attribution quality is claimed, and meetings ship with channel labels until a diarizer is selected, licensed, and evaluated.

Recordings are searchable through FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets, and playable from the sealed artifact (D-005, D-024). Each recording expands into its processing runs, and each run into a result chain rooted at that run's recognition result, so reprocessing through another model or mode inserts a new run and new results while every earlier result stays immutable and attributable (D-029). The relationship between original audio and successive results is one recording to many runs to many results, with each result naming its immediate input, the mode revision, and the model installations that produced it, which is what lets History compare two recognitions of the same audio without ambiguity. A user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion while processing is active sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter, and signals cancellation; every worker carries the recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned, or at a different generation, so a late response cannot recreate a deleted recording because the check and the insert cannot be separated. Retention is not a separate mechanism: age, size, and audio-discarding policies acquire the same leases, skip recordings held by a worker or a player, and move audio to a distinct discarded state that disables playback and re-recognition while leaving text reprocessing available (D-033). Interrupted work resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract, so a crash during recognition or rewriting leaves the committed results intact and offers a new run rather than an ambiguous partial entry (D-031). Space is reported as deleting until the last lease releases.

The model library browses and manages installed speech and language models with their declared capabilities, sizes, and owning runtime (D-022). Identity is publisher name, revision string, and a SHA-256 over the ordered weight file set, so two quantizations under one name are distinguishable and a result names exactly what produced it. Compatibility is checked before activation against the runtime descriptor covering runtime kind, version range, quantization, sample rate, and context length, and user-supplied models take the same path with the same load smoke test, so an unreadable quantization fails at install rather than mid-dictation. Installation stages, verifies, smoke-tests, then renames into an immutable content-addressed blob directory that is never written again, after which one SQLite transaction records the installation and moves the active pointer; a crash between those steps leaves an unreferenced blob that garbage collection removes, and a run pinned to the previous installation holds a lease so its weights survive activation. A failed download or import therefore cannot replace a working installation, and a failed user import stays in staging with its error attached. Model loading never triggers a download: runtimes receive absolute paths, initializers that can fetch are prohibited by a build check, and acquisition is confined to an explicitly invoked downloader on a host allowlist (D-028). Replacing a runtime has bounded effect because runtimes are separate adapter targets and helper binaries with their own measured capability descriptors and parameter schemas (D-002, D-003, D-020, D-021); common parameters render generically while runtime-specific ones may supply presentation hooks, and storage is attributable per runtime through the blob store, so removing a runtime releases its weights. Activation of a pairing exceeding the residency budget is refused with the arithmetic shown, labeled as measured or declared, and overridable by the user (D-027).

A menu bar status item is the always-available surface showing state, effective mode, recent results, and settings, complementing the recording panel (D-011, D-025). Microphone level adjustment is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator, so the common case changes no system state and has nothing to restore; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in and is restored only if the current value still equals what the app set. Optional pausing of media playback checks whether the default output device is running, using a public CoreAudio property rather than a private framework, and posts a play-pause key when something is playing. Because that evidence identifies neither the application that reacted nor whether anything paused, resume is offered as a user action in the panel and menu for ten minutes rather than performed automatically; users who accept the uncertainty can enable automatic resume, which fires only when the app posted the pause, the same output device is still default, the device is still idle, and under ten minutes have elapsed. Competing applications and manual user edits therefore produce no restoration and a note that playback or the setting was left as found, rather than the app overwriting a state someone else established. The macOS baseline and the public APIs these behaviors use are set by D-001, which holds the floor provisional until the runtime spike reports the minimum API set actually required, with anything newer behind an availability check and a defined fallback.

open_questions.question: Which speech runtime ships, can it consume a bounded credit-controlled stream, what are its cancellation latency and resume fidelity, what is its helper-process peak RSS as a function of input duration, and does the license of the weights we would offer permit distribution? RESEARCH states that documentation establishes neither accuracy nor resource behavior and flags licensing and long-recording suitability as unexamined.
open_questions.resolution: Gate F1, before the ingest port, scheduler policy, and residency budget are frozen. Thin adapters for both candidates against one corpus (30-second dictation, 10-minute session, 3-hour meeting) on the target Apple Silicon machine, recording word error rate by language, time to final transcript, helper and app peak RSS at each duration, cancellation latency at p50 and p95, and whether a resumed checkpoint reproduces the unpreempted transcript; plus a licensing review of each candidate distribution. Outputs are capability descriptors and updates to D-001, D-004, D-020, and D-027. Fallback if inconclusive: ship the whisper.cpp adapter, keep the cancel-and-restart preemption policy, and make no accuracy or latency claim.

open_questions.question: What mechanism, if any, enforces zero network access for inference helpers on the deployment baseline, given that per-process seatbelt initialization is deprecated and the application ships unsandboxed for accessibility reasons?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F2, before phase 0 exits, because it determines entitlements, the helper launch path, and the wording of the offline guarantee. Launch a helper under the strictest available restriction and assert an outbound connect fails; separately assert the helper's dependency closure imports no networking modules and its binary references no socket symbols. If no enforceable restriction exists, the guarantee stays scoped to tested structural absence, the external decoder remains off by default with its trust transfer stated, and D-028 records that outcome rather than implying system enforcement.

open_questions.question: Which insertion paths preserve existing field content and give an observable success signal in the target applications, and what pasteboard read delay does each target exhibit?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F4, before phase 1 builds the delivery path. Prototype selected-text insertion and paste-with-readback in TextEdit, Mail, Safari plain and contenteditable, Chrome, Terminal, Xcode, VS Code, Slack, and Figma, recording for each whether existing content survives, whether a change is observable, and when the pasteboard is read. The result is the per-application profile table that D-009 consumes. Fallback for any target with no observable signal: one unconfirmed attempt, no retry, deferred or disabled pasteboard restore, and a panel affordance to copy or deliver again.

open_questions.question: How much captured audio is lost when the writer is killed at an arbitrary offset, and does the packet index survive a kill during its own fsync?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F3, before phase 0 asserts recovery outcomes for the capturing and sealing states. Kill the writer at randomized offsets across chunk boundaries and mid-fsync, recover, and record the maximum lost interval and any index corruption. The measured bound becomes the approved expectation in the recovery behavior table. If the bound is worse than one chunk period plus unflushed data, shorten the chunk period and re-measure, accepting more frequent fsyncs.

open_questions.question: Which local diarizer is used for meetings, under what license, does it expose calibrated confidence suitable for an unattributed threshold, and how well do embedding matches carry edited speaker names across re-clustering when speakers leak between channels? RESEARCH names SpeakerKit within the Argmax package and notes that its default initialization may download models.
open_questions.resolution: Resolve before the diarization half of phase 8, since the meetings data model depends on it. Review the license, confirm that a model-folder configuration prevents any download, and evaluate per-segment outputs on a labeled internal meeting set reporting diarization error rate, the below-threshold rate, and behavior with speaker echo when headphones are not used. If no usable confidence exists, meetings ship with channel labels only; the schema already represents that state and phase 8 delivers capture and notes regardless.

open_questions.question: Which languages get validator packs at ship, and how often does the fail-closed path deny rewriting to users who wanted it?
open_questions.resolution: Ship the English pack in phase 3 and add packs in phase 9 driven by measured fallback rates per language. If the denial rate is high for a language with good recognition, that language's pack moves ahead of other phase 9 work; the per-mode override exists in the meantime and records itself on the result.

open_questions.question: Which browsers expose the current URL through accessibility, and which need automation permission or provide nothing?
open_questions.resolution: Enumerate per browser in phase 6 and record a dated table. The rule engine treats an unreadable URL as a non-match, so an incomplete table degrades to bundle-identifier rules and the default mode.

open_questions.question: Is FTS5 compiled into the system SQLite on the chosen baseline?
open_questions.resolution: A runtime check during phase 0 setup. If absent, build GRDB against a bundled SQLite, accepting a larger binary and an update obligation, and record the change against D-005.

open_questions.question: Is an 8B-class instruct model at 4-bit quantization good enough for Email and Meeting notes on the 16 GB target, or does a smaller model with tighter prompts do better once the contract validator is applied?
open_questions.resolution: Score two or three sizes against the fidelity corpus in phase 4 using the human rubric, recording validator fallback rates per model. The result sets the recommended default pairing; model selection is per mode either way, so a wrong default is a settings change.

open_questions.question: Can the provisional live pass run alongside capture without dropping frames or degrading the final pass on the target machine?
open_questions.resolution: Measure in phase 2 beside the runtime work: capture with and without the provisional pass, comparing dropped frame counts, final word error rate, and time to final transcript. If the cost is material, the preview degrades to waveform plus a voice-activity indicator, which the panel already has a state for.
